mainTopic: שילוח הקן: unfit fledglings, unresolved questions, the male קורא, and a mother hovering or perched above the nest
overview: The amud continues the laws of שילוח הקן. It first shows that the mother bird is not judged like the fledglings, and אביי rereads a ברייתא so it fits רב כהנא's rule that טרפה fledglings are exempt. Next come several questions: רב הושעיא asks about partly slaughtered fledglings, רבי ירמיה asks about things lying between the mother and the eggs, and רבי זירא asks about a bird sitting on another kosher species' eggs. The first two end in תיקו, and אביי's attempted proof for רבי זירא's question is rejected. The גמרא then explains the משנה's מחלוקת about a male קורא. רבי אליעזר learns from the word 'brooding' that it must be sent away, and רבי אלעזר limits the argument to the male קורא alone. A new משנה teaches that a hovering mother counts if her wings touch the nest, that even one egg is enough, and that unfertilized eggs and chicks that can fly are excluded. Finally the גמרא discusses רב's ruling about a bird perched on tree branches above the nest, in two versions of a debate over a ברייתא. The second version ends with a challenge that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The mother is not compared to the fledglings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea that the mother bird should be treated like the fledglings. If she were, the word צפור would not be needed to exclude a non-kosher bird.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why do I need the word 'צפור' to exclude a non-kosher bird?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the suggestion that the mother should follow the same rule as the fledglings. It proves that this comparison is wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose the mother were judged like the fledglings. Then we would already know that a non-kosher mother is exempt, because non-kosher fledglings are not 'for yourself'. Since the תורה still needed the word צפור to exclude a non-kosher bird, the mother must have her own rules and is not simply compared to the fledglings.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: introduces a problem that follows from the suggestion
Bird: the word in the פסוק of שילוח הקן, understood as meaning a kosher bird
To exclude
A non-kosher bird
Why do I need it? This points out that a word in the פסוק would be extra

phrases.english: If so, the word 'bird'
to exclude a non-kosher bird, why do I need it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, ״צִפּוֹר״ לְמַעוֹטֵי עוֹף טָמֵא לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the earlier suggestion (just before this section) that the mother should be compared to the fledglings
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects comparing the mother bird to the fledglings
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The comparison would make the word צפור extra, because a non-kosher bird would already be excluded

steps.title: A ברייתא says a טרפה case is obligated
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to say fledglings which are טרפה do require שילוח הקן. This appears to contradict רב כהנא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But wasn't it taught: a mother of fledglings, טרפה, is obligated in sending away!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב כהנא with a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite of his rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא said that fledglings which are טרפה do not require sending the mother away. The ברייתא's words 'mother of fledglings, טרפה' sound as if the fledglings are טרפה and yet there is still an obligation. That would directly contradict רב כהנא.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal or bird with a fatal defect, which may not be eaten even if slaughtered
Sending away: the מצוה of sending away the mother bird
Fledglings, young birds
Obligated

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught: a mother of fledglings that is a tereifa –
phrases.notes: The wording is unclear: is the mother טרפה or the fledglings? The challenge reads it as the fledglings.

phrases.english: one is obligated to send her away!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns back to challenge רב כהנא's basic rule
steps.kashyaTarget: רב כהנא's rule that fledglings which are טרפה do not require שילוח הקן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא seems to require sending the mother away even when the fledglings are טרפה

steps.title: אביי: the mother is the טרפה
steps.stepSummary: אביי rereads the ברייתא. The word טרפה describes the mother, not the fledglings, so the ברייתא fits רב כהנא.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: this is what it means: a fledgling whose mother is a טרפה, one is obligated to send away.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge by explaining the ברייתא differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to אביי, the ברייתא is talking about healthy fledglings whose mother is טרפה. The fledglings can still be eaten, so they count as 'for yourself' and the מצוה applies. This also fits step 1: the mother's own status does not decide the matter.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means: introduces a new reading of a source
Whose mother

steps.whatToRemember: A fledgling that is טרפה does not require שילוח הקן, but if only the mother is טרפה, the obligation still applies.

phrases.english: Abaye said: this is what it is saying –
a fledgling whose mother is a tereifa
one is obligated to send her away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to mean that the fledglings were טרפה
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא means that the mother is טרפה and the fledglings are fine

steps.title: רב הושעיא asks about a partly slaughtered fledgling
steps.stepSummary: רב הושעיא asks about someone who reached into the nest and cut only a minority of the fledglings' סימנים. Is he still obligated to send the mother away?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הושעיא asked: if someone reached into the nest and cut a minority of the סימנים, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. It builds on רב כהנא's rule about fledglings that are not fit to eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Cutting only a minority of the סימנים is not a finished שחיטה, and it leaves the bird injured. The question is whether this half-finished state counts as 'not for yourself', which would mean no obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: Asked a question, raised a doubt
Nest
A minority of the two organs (windpipe and food pipe) that are cut in שחיטה
What is the law?

phrases.english: Rav Hoshaya asked:
if he stretched his hand into the nest,
and slaughtered a minority of the simanim, what is the law?
phrases.notes: He cut the fledglings' סימנים, not the mother's.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question built on רב כהנא's principle
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a fledgling with a partly cut set of סימנים still require sending the mother away?

steps.title: The two sides of the question
steps.stepSummary: One side: if left as they are, the fledglings would become טרפה, so they are not 'for yourself'. Other side: he can still finish the שחיטה, so they count as 'take for yourself'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do we say: since if he leaves them they will become טרפה, and we need 'for you and not for your dogs', he is exempt? Or perhaps, since he is able to finish the שחיטה, we read 'take for yourself' about it, and he is obligated?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out both possible ways of looking at רב הושעיא's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first side looks at what the bird will become if it is left alone: a טרפה, fit only for dogs. The second side looks at what the person can still do: finish the שחיטה and make the bird kosher to eat. The question is which of these counts.

keyTerms.meaning: Do we say...? This opens the first side of a question
Or perhaps: opens the second side
For you and not for your dogs: the reading of 'תקח לך' that says the fledglings must be fit to eat
In his power, able to do it

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides agree on רב כהנא's rule that a טרפה fledgling is exempt. They only disagree on whether a bird that is not yet טרפה, but will become one, counts as 'for your dogs'.

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן: כֵּיוָן דְּאִילּוּ שָׁבֵיק לְהוּ מִטַּרְפִי,
phrases.english: Do we say: since if he were to leave them they would become tereifot,
and we require 'for you and not for your dogs',

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, כֵּיוָן דִּבְיָדוֹ לְמִגְמַר שְׁחִיטָה,
phrases.english: or perhaps, since it is in his power to complete the slaughter,
we call this 'take for yourself',
and he is obligated to send her away?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the two sides of רב הושעיא's question
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do we judge the bird by what it will become if left alone, or by what he can still do to it?

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: No answer is found, so the question is left open with תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand (unresolved).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends רב הושעיא's question without deciding it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו means the question stays open. Neither side is proven.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question remains unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: Whether partly slaughtered fledglings require sending the mother away is left as an open question (תיקו).

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question without an answer
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב הושעיא's question about partly cut סימנים is left unresolved

steps.title: Does a rag or loose feathers block the mother from the eggs?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks whether a rag or loose wing feathers lying between the mother bird and the eggs count as a barrier.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה asked: if a rag is between the mother and the eggs, does it block her? If wing feathers are there, do they block her?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה starts a new set of questions. He asks whether something lying between the mother bird and her eggs stops her from counting as 'sitting on' them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה obligates sending away the mother when she is sitting on the young or the eggs. If a rag or loose feathers count as a barrier, she is not truly sitting on the eggs, and there would be no obligation. The question is whether this kind of thing blocks her or just counts as part of the nest.

keyTerms.meaning: A rag or piece of cloth
Something that blocks or separates; a barrier
Wings; here, loose feathers from a bird's wings
What is the law? (opens a question)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya asked:
A rag: does it count as a barrier?
Wing feathers: do they count as a barrier?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה: מַטְלֵית מַהוּ שֶׁתָּחוֹץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New question, separate from רב הושעיא's question that ended in תיקו
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a rag or loose feathers between the mother and the eggs count as a barrier that cancels the obligation

steps.title: More possible barriers: bad eggs, a second layer of eggs, a male bird
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה continues with three more cases: unfertilized eggs, two layers of eggs, and a male bird sitting between the female and the eggs.
steps.simpleTranslation: What if unfertilized eggs are in between? What if there are two layers of eggs, one on top of the other? What if a male sits on the eggs and the female sits on the male?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה adds three more cases where something lies between the mother and the eggs. These are harder cases, because the thing in between is itself part of the nest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unfertilized eggs will never hatch, so they may act like a rag. The top layer of good eggs is itself under the mother, but it might still block her from the bottom layer. A male bird is a living part of the nest, yet the female is not touching the eggs directly.

keyTerms.meaning: Unfertilized eggs that will not hatch
Layers or rows of eggs
Male bird / female bird

phrases.english: Unfertilized eggs: what is the law?
phrases.notes: He means unfertilized eggs lying between the mother and the good eggs.

phrases.english: Two layers of eggs
one on top of the other: what is the law?
A male on top of the eggs
and a female on top of the male: what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבי ירמיה's list of possible barriers
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether unfertilized eggs, an upper layer of eggs, or a male bird count as a barrier between the mother and the eggs

steps.title: All of רבי ירמיה's questions stay unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finds no answer, so all of רבי ירמיה's questions are left open.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes רבי ירמיה's whole list with תיקו. No answer was found for any of the cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו means the question stays open. It does not mean the answer is 'no' or 'yes'. The cases of a rag, feathers, unfertilized eggs, layered eggs, and a male bird all stay unresolved.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question is left unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: רבי ירמיה's questions about barriers between the mother and the eggs all end in תיקו. None of them is decided.

phrases.english: Let it stand unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the questions of steps 7–8
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All of רבי ירמיה's barrier questions remain unresolved

steps.title: A pigeon on a תסיל's eggs, or the reverse
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא asks what the law is when one kosher species sits on the eggs of a different but similar kosher species.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא asked: if a יונה sits on the eggs of a תסיל, what is the law? If a תסיל sits on the eggs of a יונה, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא asks a new question. Must the bird be sent away if it is sitting on eggs that are not from its own species?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both birds are kosher and look alike, but the mother is not sitting on her own kind's eggs. The question is whether שילוח הקן needs the mother to be the eggs' real mother, or at least the same species. Or is it enough that she is a kosher bird sitting on kosher eggs?

keyTerms.meaning: A pigeon or dove
A kosher bird that looks like a pigeon
The מצוה of sending away the mother bird from the nest

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira asked:
A pigeon on the eggs of a tasil: what is the law?
A tasil on the eggs of a pigeon: what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַבִּי זֵירָא: יוֹנָה עַל בֵּיצֵי תָסִיל, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question, separate from רבי ירמיה's barrier questions
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a kosher bird sitting on another kosher species' eggs must be sent away

steps.title: אביי tries to answer from the משנה
steps.stepSummary: אביי quotes the משנה: a טמא bird on טהור eggs, or the reverse, is exempt. That suggests a טהור bird on other טהור eggs is obligated.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Come and hear. A non-kosher bird sitting on a kosher bird's eggs, or a kosher bird sitting on a non-kosher bird's eggs, is exempt from sending. That means a kosher bird on kosher eggs is obligated!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי tries to answer רבי זירא's question from the משנה. He uses an inference from what the משנה chose to say.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only exempts mixed cases of טמא and טהור. אביי reasons that if both are טהור, even from different species, the obligation applies. That would mean a יונה on a תסיל's eggs must be sent away.

keyTerms.meaning: A non-kosher bird
A kosher bird
Sitting or resting on (the eggs)
Exempt
Obligated

phrases.english: Abaye said: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: עוֹף טָמֵא רוֹבֵץ עַל בֵּיצֵי עוֹף טָהוֹר,
phrases.english: a non-kosher bird sitting on the eggs of a kosher bird,

phrases.aramaic: וְטָהוֹר רוֹבֵץ עַל בֵּיצֵי עוֹף טָמֵא –
phrases.english: or a kosher bird sitting on the eggs of a non-kosher bird:
he is exempt from sending it away.
So a kosher bird on kosher eggs means he is obligated!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer רבי זירא's question
steps.raayaObject: That a kosher bird on another kosher species' eggs must be sent away
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה exempting a טמא/טהור mix, which implies obligation when both are טהור

steps.title: Maybe the משנה is only about a קורא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof: the משנה's implied case may only be a קורא, a bird that normally sits on other birds' eggs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps it means a קורא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on אביי's proof. It suggests the implied case in the משנה is limited to one special bird.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קורא normally sits on other birds' eggs, so for it this is normal nesting, and the obligation applies. That says nothing about a יונה or a תסיל, which normally sit only on their own eggs. So רבי זירא's question is still open.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps; used to push back on a proof
A bird (often translated as a pheasant) known for sitting on other birds' eggs

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying a תסיל on a יונה's eggs is exempt. It only shows that אביי's proof doesn't settle the question.

phrases.english: Perhaps it is talking about a kore.
phrases.notes: A קורא is a bird that normally sits on eggs that aren't its own, so for it this is normal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects אביי's proof
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof is rejected. The question itself stays open.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה's implied obligation may be limited to a קורא, a bird whose nature is to sit on other birds' eggs.

steps.title: The משנה's case of a male קורא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: for a male קורא sitting on eggs, רבי אליעזר obligates sending it away and חכמים exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: A male pheasant (sitting on the eggs): רבי אליעזר says you are obligated to send it away, and the חכמים say you are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה to set up a discussion about it. Here a male קורא sits on eggs, and the תנאים argue whether you must send it away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally שילוח הקן is about the mother bird. In this case a male bird is doing the sitting. רבי אליעזר says that still counts, and חכמים say it does not.

keyTerms.meaning: A type of bird (often called a pheasant). It is known for sitting on eggs.
Male
Says you are obligated
They say you are exempt

phrases.english: A male pheasant (sitting on eggs),
Rabbi Eliezer obligates (sending it away)
and the Sages exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: קוֹרֵא זָכָר, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר מְחַיֵּיב וַחֲכָמִים פּוֹטְרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the open questions to a new line of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Male קורא: רבי אליעזר obligates sending it away; חכמים exempt.

steps.title: What is רבי אליעזר's reason?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו asks why רבי אליעזר obligates sending away a male bird.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: What is the reason of רבי אליעזר?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו asks where רבי אליעזר gets his opinion. This question sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק speaks about a mother bird, so including a male bird needs a source. רבי אבהו is looking for that source.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said:
What is the reason of Rabbi Eliezer?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of רבי אליעזר's view in the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural basis for counting a male קורא's sitting

steps.title: A גזירה שוה from the word 'brooding'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר learns from the word 'דגר' (brooding), which is used for the male קורא in ירמיהו and for a nesting female bird in ישעיהו.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is learned from 'brooding' and 'brooding.' It is written here: 'The קורא broods but did not give birth,' and it is written there: 'and hatch, and brood under her shadow.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו answers his own question with a גזירה שוה. The same word 'brooding' appears about a male קורא and about a mother bird.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ירמיהו the male קורא 'broods' even though he did not lay the eggs. In ישעיהו a female bird 'broods' on her nest. The shared word teaches that the male's brooding counts like the female's, so he must be sent away too.

keyTerms.meaning: Learning one case from another because the same word appears in both
Brooding: sitting on eggs to warm them
It is written here... and it is written there (how a גזירה שוה is set up)

phrases.english: It is learned from 'brooding' and 'brooding,'
phrases.notes: The same word shows up in two פסוקים, so we learn one from the other.

phrases.english: it is written here
'The pheasant broods, but did not give birth,'
and it is written there
'and she hatches, and broods under her shadow.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה on 'דגר' makes the male קורא's brooding count like a mother bird's.

steps.title: Everyone agrees about a female קורא
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says the argument is only about a male קורא; for a female קורא, all agree you must send it away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: The argument is about a male קורא, but with a female קורא, everyone agrees you are obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר limits the מחלוקת. It covers only a male קורא, and with a female קורא even חכמים require sending it away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This tells us what חכמים hold. They do not exempt the קורא species as a whole. They only exempt the male.

keyTerms.meaning: A disagreement
Female
Everyone agrees
Obligated

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up רבי אלעזר (the אמורא making this ruling) with רבי אליעזר (the תנא in the משנה). The names look almost the same.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
The disagreement is about a male pheasant,
but with a female pheasant,
everyone agrees one is obligated.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: מַחְלוֹקֶת בְּקוֹרֵא זָכָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines how far the משנה's מחלוקת reaches
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a female קורא, all agree you must send it away.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי אלעזר needed to say this, since the משנה clearly says 'male.'
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious! We learned 'a male קורא' in the משנה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אלעזר's ruling as unnecessary. The משנה already says the argument is about a male.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה names a male, it seems clear that a female is a different case. So what is רבי אלעזר adding?

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (a challenge saying a statement adds nothing)

phrases.english: That is obvious!
We learned (in the משנה) 'a male pheasant'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 16 as unnecessary
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's word 'male' already implies that a female is not part of the argument.

steps.title: Maybe 'male' only showed how far רבי אליעזר goes
steps.stepSummary: Without רבי אלעזר, we might think חכמים exempt even a female קורא, and that the משנה said 'male' only to show how far רבי אליעזר goes.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said that the רבנן exempt even a female קורא, and that the משנה says 'male' only to show you how far רבי אליעזר goes. So רבי אלעזר teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word 'male' could have been read another way. רבי אלעזר's ruling removes that wrong reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Maybe the משנה chose the male case to show that רבי אליעזר obligates even a male. If so, חכמים might exempt every קורא. רבי אלעזר teaches that חכמים agree about the female.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces a mistaken idea)
To show you how far his opinion goes
It teaches us (that this is not so)

phrases.english: so he teaches us (that this is not so).

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא רַבָּנַן אֲפִילּוּ קוֹרֵא נְקֵבָה פָּטְרִי

steps.terutzMaskana: חכמים agree that you must send away a female קורא.

steps.title: Everyone agrees an ordinary male bird is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר adds that for males of other birds, all agree you are exempt; the argument is only about a male קורא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אלעזר said: The argument is about a male קורא, but with an ordinary male bird, everyone agrees you are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר limits the argument from the other side. Even רבי אליעזר exempts ordinary male birds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר's obligation applies only to the male קורא. The פסוק says that bird 'broods,' and other male birds have no such source.

keyTerms.meaning: An ordinary male bird of any other kind
Exempt

phrases.english: And Rabbi Elazar said:
The disagreement is about a male pheasant,
but with an ordinary male bird,
everyone agrees one is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second ruling of רבי אלעזר limiting the מחלוקת from the other side
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Ordinary male birds: all agree you are exempt.

steps.title: Isn't this obvious too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא again asks why this was needed, since the משנה says 'male קורא' and not just 'male.'
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious! We learned 'a male קורא' in the משנה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes the same challenge against the second ruling. The משנה already names the קורא specifically.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the משנה specifies a קורא, it seems clear that other male birds are not part of the argument.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה already says 'male קורא'

phrases.english: That is obvious!
We learned (in the משנה) 'a male pheasant'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 19 as unnecessary
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's word 'קורא' already leaves other male birds out of the argument.

steps.title: Maybe 'קורא' only showed how far חכמים go
steps.stepSummary: Without רבי אלעזר, we might think רבי אליעזר obligates every male bird, and that the משנה said 'קורא' only to show that חכמים exempt even a קורא.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said that רבי אליעזר obligates even an ordinary male bird, and that the משנה says 'male קורא' to show how far the רבנן go. So רבי אלעזר teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers in the same way, but from the other side. The word 'קורא' could have been read as showing how far חכמים go.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קורא actually broods, so it is the hardest case to exempt. Maybe the משנה chose it to show that חכמים exempt even this bird, while רבי אליעזר obligates all males. רבי אלעזר teaches that רבי אליעזר exempts ordinary males.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second פשיטא challenge

steps.terutzMaskana: Even רבי אליעזר exempts ordinary male birds.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא states that an ordinary male bird is exempt, and that only a male קורא is in dispute.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way in a ברייתא: An ordinary male bird is exempt. A male קורא: רבי אליעזר obligates and the חכמים exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says exactly what רבי אלעזר said in his second ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא states without any argument that an ordinary male is exempt. Only then does it bring the מחלוקת about the male קורא. This shows that even רבי אליעזר agrees about ordinary males.

keyTerms.meaning: Also like this (a source that supports what was just said)
A teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא confirms that רבי אליעזר's obligation applies only to the male קורא, not to male birds in general.

phrases.english: It was also taught this way (in a ברייתא):
An ordinary male bird is exempt;
a male pheasant: Rabbi Eliezer obligates,
and the Sages exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for רבי אלעזר's second ruling
steps.raayaObject: רבי אלעזר's ruling that all agree an ordinary male bird is exempt
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that lists the ordinary male as exempt without any dispute

steps.title: A hovering mother bird counts only if her wings touch the nest
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that a hovering mother bird must be sent away if her wings touch the nest, but not if they don't.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the mother bird was hovering: when her wings touch the nest, you must send her away. When her wings don't touch the nest, you don't have to.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It deals with a mother bird that is hovering in the air over her nest instead of sitting on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מצוה of שילוח הקן normally applies when the mother is on the nest. The משנה says a hovering bird can still count, but only if her wings are in contact with the nest. With no contact, she is not considered "on" the nest at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (the abbreviation מַתְנִי׳ marks where it begins)
Hovering, fluttering in the air
Her wings are touching
Obligated to send away (the mother bird)
Exempt from sending away

phrases.english: MISHNA: If the mother bird was hovering,
when her wings are touching the nest,
one is obligated to send her away.
If her wings are not touching the nest,
one is exempt from sending her away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the previous discussion about male birds and the קורא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A hovering mother bird is included in שילוח הקן only if her wings touch the nest.

steps.title: Even a single egg or fledgling is enough
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that even one fledgling or one egg obligates you, because the פסוק says "nest" with no minimum.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even if there is only one fledgling or one egg, you must send away the mother, because the פסוק says "nest," meaning any nest at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with a second rule: you don't need a full nest of many eggs for the מצוה to apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think the plural words "fledglings" and "eggs" in the פסוק require at least two. The משנה points to the word קן, which sets no number, so a nest with just one egg or chick still counts.

keyTerms.meaning: A fledgling, a baby bird
An egg
A nest
In any case, of any kind

phrases.english: If there is only one fledgling there
or one egg,
one is obligated to send her away,
as it is stated: "Nest,"
a nest of any kind.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין שָׁם אֶלָּא אֶפְרוֹחַ אֶחָד אוֹ בֵּיצָה אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second rule in the same משנה, about how many eggs or chicks are needed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One egg or one fledgling is enough to obligate שילוח הקן.

steps.title: Flying fledglings and unfertilized eggs are excluded
steps.stepSummary: The משנה exempts fledglings that can fly and eggs that will never hatch, learning this by comparing eggs and fledglings in the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the fledglings can already fly, or the eggs are unfertilized, you don't have to send away the mother. The פסוק puts fledglings and eggs side by side. Just as fledglings are alive, the eggs must be able to produce living chicks, so unfertilized eggs are out. And just as eggs need their mother, the fledglings must still need their mother, so chicks that can fly are out.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives its third rule, which is an exclusion. It brings a two-way comparison from the פסוק to prove it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says "upon the fledglings or upon the eggs," so each one teaches something about the other. From fledglings we learn eggs must be able to live, which excludes unfertilized eggs. From eggs we learn the fledglings must still depend on the mother, which excludes chicks that can fly.

keyTerms.meaning: Fledglings old enough to fly
Unfertilized eggs that will never hatch
Resting, crouching (on the nest)
Living, able to survive
This excludes, these are left out

steps.whatToRemember: The מצוה needs a real, dependent nest: eggs that can hatch and chicks that still need their mother.

phrases.english: If there were fledglings that can fly,
or unfertilized eggs,
one is exempt from sending her away,
as it is stated: "And the mother is resting
upon the fledglings or upon the eggs."
Just as fledglings are living,
so too the eggs must be able to produce living chicks;
this excludes unfertilized eggs.
And just as the eggs need their mother,
so too the fledglings must be ones that need their mother;
this excludes fledglings that can fly.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיוּ שָׁם אֶפְרוֹחִים מַפְרִיחִים אוֹ בֵּיצִים מוּזָרוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After saying even one egg counts, the משנה limits which eggs and chicks qualify.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Unfertilized eggs and fledglings able to fly are exempt from שילוח הקן, derived from the side-by-side comparison of eggs and fledglings in the פסוק.

steps.title: A ברייתא: "resting" includes a hovering bird whose wings touch
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that uses the word רובצת both to exclude a hovering bird and to include one whose wings touch the nest.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: "Resting," and not hovering. You might think that even if her wings touch the nest she is exempt? So the פסוק says "resting," to include that case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and brings a ברייתא that gives the source for the משנה's first rule about a hovering bird.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first, רובצת seems to exclude any bird not sitting on the nest. The ברייתא then says the same word actually includes a hovering bird whose wings touch the nest. How one word does both is not yet explained, which sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: One might have thought
Therefore the פסוק says (to teach otherwise)

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
"Resting," and not hovering.
One might think she is exempt even if her wings are touching the nest?
Therefore the פסוק says: "Resting."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the scriptural source for the משנה's rule about a hovering bird in step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word רובצת excludes a hovering bird, but includes one whose wings touch the nest.

steps.title: How does "resting" teach this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the word רובצת shows that a bird whose wings touch the nest is included.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the derivation?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question about the ברייתא. It wants to know how the word רובצת proves the rule, and this sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא used רובצת both to exclude hovering and to include wings touching. The גמרא asks what exactly in this word points to the wider meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the derivation? How is this learned?

phrases.english: What is the derivation?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the method of the ברייתא in step 26.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the word רובצת includes a hovering bird whose wings touch the nest.

steps.title: The תורה said "resting," not "sitting"
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that since the פסוק did not say יושבת, "resting" must be a wider word that includes wings touching.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn it from the fact that the פסוק does not say "sitting."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by pointing to the word the תורה chose not to use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the תורה only meant a bird sitting right on the nest, it would have written יושבת. Choosing רובצת shows a broader idea of resting over the nest, which includes a bird whose wings touch it.

keyTerms.meaning: From the fact that it is not written
Sitting

steps.confusionAlert: רובצת does two jobs here. It excludes a bird that is fully in the air, yet includes one whose wings touch, because it is broader than "sitting."

phrases.english: From the fact that "sitting" is not written.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The תורה chose רובצת over יושבת, showing that contact with the nest, not sitting on it, is enough.

steps.title: A bird sitting between two branches
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that a mother bird perched between two branches above the nest counts only if she would fall onto the nest when the branches give way.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: If the mother bird was sitting between two tree branches, we look. If she would fall onto the eggs or chicks if the branches gave way, you must send her away. If not, you are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling about a tricky case: a mother bird resting on branches above the nest instead of on the nest itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bird is not touching the nest, so we need a test for whether she counts as "resting" on it. רב says to picture the branches giving way. If she would land on the eggs or chicks, she counts as over them and the מצוה applies; if she would fall to the side, it does not.

keyTerms.meaning: Tree branches
We look, we examine
Slip down, drop out

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a practical test for a bird that is near the nest but not touching it, building on the idea that רובצת is wider than plain sitting.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda says that Rav says:

phrases.aramaic: הָיְתָה יוֹשֶׁבֶת בֵּין שְׁנֵי רוֹבְדֵי אִילָן –
phrases.english: If the mother bird was sitting between two tree branches,
we look: in any case where, if she were to slip down,
she would fall upon them,
one is obligated to send her away;
and if not, one is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב הָיְתָה יוֹשֶׁבֶת בֵּין שְׁנֵי רוֹבְדֵי אִילָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the idea of "resting over the nest" to a new case where the bird sits on branches above it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bird perched between branches is included if she would fall onto the eggs or chicks were the branches to give way; otherwise she is exempt.

steps.title: A ברייתא is brought against רב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא about a bird sitting between the young, above them, or hovering, in order to challenge רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged רב: If the mother was sitting between them, one is exempt from sending her away. If she was above them, one must send her away. If she was hovering, even if her wings touch the nest, one is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to attack רב's ruling about a bird perched on branches. This step only quotes the source. The actual attack comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists three cases. Between the young means exempt, above them means obligated, and hovering means exempt even if the wings touch. The challenge will depend on what 'above them' means.

keyTerms.meaning: Between them, sitting among the eggs or chicks rather than on top
Above them, on top of them
Hovering, flying over the nest
Exempt from sending away the mother bird

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
phrases.notes: This is a challenge to רב from step 29, who ruled that a bird perched on branches above the nest can count.

phrases.english: If she was sitting between them, one is exempt from sending her away,
if she was above them, one is obligated to send her away,
if she was hovering,

phrases.english: even if her wings are touching the nest, one is exempt from sending her away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to challenge רב's ruling in step 29.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that a bird perched on branches above the nest can count
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup only. The attack is built in the next step.

steps.title: Reading 'above them' as touching
steps.stepSummary: The challenger compares 'above' to 'between': both involve touching, so a bird on branches that does not touch is exempt, against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't 'above them' just like 'between them'? Just as 'between them' means she touches them, so too 'above them' means she touches them. But a bird on tree branches would be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the ברייתא contradicts רב. If 'above them' means touching, then a bird sitting on branches without touching would be exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two cases are read as a pair. Sitting between the young clearly involves touching, so sitting above them should also mean touching. The result is that only touching counts, and a bird on branches is exempt, which contradicts רב.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it that...? It introduces a suggested reading that leads to a challenge
Similar to, parallel with
Tree branches, here the case of a bird perched on branches above the nest

is similar to 'between them':
just as 'between them' is where she touches them,

steps.title: 'Above them' means not touching from above
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the challenge. The comparison works the other way: neither case rests on top of the young, so 'above them' is the branches case.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. 'Above them' is like 'between them' in this way: just as 'between them' means she is not resting on top of them, so too 'above them' means she is not resting on top of them. That is the case of tree branches.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps the comparison but turns it around. The ברייתא's 'above them' is exactly the bird on branches, and she is obligated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sitting between the young touches them from the side, not from on top. So 'above them' also means not resting on top, which describes perching on branches over the nest. The ברייתא now supports רב instead of contradicting him.

keyTerms.meaning: Touching them from on top, resting on them
And that is exactly...

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides use the same comparison, 'above is like between.' They disagree only about what the two cases share: touching, or not resting on top.

phrases.english: No. 'Above them' is similar to 'between them' this way:
just as 'between them' is where she is not touching them from on top,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּבֵּיהֶן – דְּלֹא נָגְעָה עֲלַיְיהוּ,
phrases.english: so too 'above them' is where she is not touching them from on top,
and that is the case of tree branches.

steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The reading of 'above them' as touching

steps.title: Proof from the ברייתא's choice of examples
steps.stepSummary: If a bird on branches were exempt, the ברייתא would have taught that case, and hovering would follow even more so.
steps.simpleTranslation: This also makes sense. If you thought a bird on branches is exempt, then instead of teaching that a hovering bird is exempt even when her wings touch the nest, it should have taught that a bird on branches is exempt. A hovering bird would then be exempt all the more so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports its rejection by looking at which example the ברייתא chose. This shows the branches case must be obligated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A bird resting on branches is closer to the nest than a hovering bird. If even she were exempt, teaching her case would teach the hovering case automatically. Since the ברייתא taught hovering instead, the branches bird must be obligated, just as רב said.

for if it should enter your mind

then instead of teaching: if she was hovering,

phrases.english: even if her wings are touching the nest, one is exempt from sending her away,
let it teach the case of tree branches,
and all the more so a hovering bird!

steps.raayaObject: That 'above them' in the ברייתא is the branches case, and she is obligated

steps.title: The hovering case was needed for its own lesson
steps.stepSummary: The proof from step 33 is rejected. The ברייתא had to mention a hovering bird to teach that even if her wings touch the nest, there is no obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case of a hovering bird was needed to teach that even if her wings touch the nest, one is exempt from sending her away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from step 33. It explains why the ברייתא mentioned a hovering bird even if a bird on branches would also be exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 33 argued that if a bird on branches were exempt, the ברייתא would have taught that case instead of hovering. The answer is that hovering adds something new: even when her wings touch the nest, she is still exempt. A bird on branches might not touch the nest at all, so the branches case could not teach that lesson.

keyTerms.meaning: Hovering or flying over the nest
It was needed for him, meaning the תנא had a reason to teach it
Her wings are touching
Exempt from the מצוה of sending away the mother

phrases.english: The hovering case was needed for him [to teach],

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 33.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the ברייתא's choice of cases. It does not prove that רב is right or wrong.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the hovering case added nothing. In fact it teaches that touching wings alone do not create an obligation.

steps.title: The משנה says touching wings do obligate
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא itself. Our משנה rules that when the wings touch the nest, one must send the mother away.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned in the משנה: when her wings touch the nest, one is obligated to send her away!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now attacks the ברייתא. Its ruling seems to contradict our משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says a hovering bird whose wings touch the nest is exempt. The משנה says that when her wings touch the nest, there is an obligation. The two sources seem to rule in opposite ways on the very same case.

keyTerms.meaning: Obligated to send away the mother bird
The nest
At a time when, meaning whenever this is the case

phrases.english: But didn't we learn [in the משנה]:
When her wings are touching the nest,
one is obligated to send [her] away!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After establishing what the ברייתא teaches, the גמרא questions whether the ברייתא fits the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a hovering bird with touching wings is exempt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה outranks a ברייתא. The משנה obligates when the wings touch the nest, which directly contradicts the ברייתא.

steps.title: The ברייתא means touching from the side
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה explains that the ברייתא is talking about wings that touch the nest from the side. The משנה is talking about touching from above.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: When the ברייתא teaches this, it is talking about a bird touching the nest from the side.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה answers the contradiction. He shows that the two sources are talking about different kinds of touching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, the wings brush the nest from the side, so the bird is not over the young, and she is exempt. In the משנה, the bird hovers directly above, and her wings touch from on top, so she is obligated. The key factor is whether she is above the young.

keyTerms.meaning: A taught source. Here it refers to the ברייתא, not our משנה
Touching
From the side

steps.confusionAlert: Here the word מתניתא does NOT mean our משנה. It refers to the ברייתא about the hovering bird.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:
When the teaching states [this],
phrases.notes: "The teaching" here is the ברייתא about the hovering bird, not our משנה.

phrases.english: it is about [wings] touching from the side.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה: כִּי קָתָנֵי מַתְנִיתָא בְּנוֹגֵעַ מִן הַצַּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source refers to a different situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seemed to be talking about the same kind of touching, so they appeared to contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא exempts touching from the side. The משנה obligates touching from above.
steps.whatToRemember: Touching the nest is not enough by itself. What matters is whether the bird is over the young: touching from above obligates, touching from the side does not.

steps.title: Second version: the ברייתא offered as support for רב
steps.stepSummary: A second version of the discussion presents the same ברייתא as possible support for רב. The ברייתא lists three cases: between the young, above them, and hovering.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say the discussion went like this: Let us say a ברייתא supports רב. If she was sitting between them, one is exempt. If above them, one is obligated. If she was hovering, even with her wings touching the nest, one is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a second version of the discussion. Here the same ברייתא is brought to help רב instead of to challenge him. This step quotes the ברייתא, and the next step will draw the proof from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version (steps 30–33), this ברייתא was used to attack רב. In this version, the very same text is read as supporting him. Here the case of "between them" will be understood as a bird that does not rest on top of the young.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say it supports him
Between them, among the eggs or chicks
On top of them, above them

phrases.english: There are those who say [the discussion went]:
Let us say [this] supports him:
If she was sitting between them,
one is exempt from sending [her] away;
above them, one is obligated to send [her] away;
if she was hovering,
even if her wings are touching the nest,
one is exempt from sending [her] away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restarts the discussion in a second version, using the ברייתא from step 30 as support for רב rather than as a challenge.
steps.raayaObject: רב's ruling that a mother bird on branches above the nest can create an obligation.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא listing three cases: between the young, above them, and hovering.

steps.title: "Above them" is the tree-branches case
steps.stepSummary: The proof: "above them" should be read like "between them," meaning not resting on the young. That describes a bird on branches, and the ברייתא obligates in that case, just as רב says.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't it that "above them" is like "between them"? Just as "between them" means she is not resting on top of them, so too "above them" means she is not resting on them. And that is the case of the tree branches!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the proof for רב from the ברייתא it just quoted. It reads "above them" as a bird on branches over the nest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two cases are compared: in "between them" she does not rest on the young. So in "above them" she also does not rest on them, and she must be held up by something, namely branches. Since the ברייתא says "above them" is obligated, it supports רב's ruling about branches.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it not? This opens a suggested reading meant as a proof
Similar to, parallel with
Touching (resting) on top of them
Tree branches

steps.whatToRemember: In this second version, the ברייתא's "above them" means a bird on branches over the nest, and it is obligated, which matches רב.

phrases.english: Is it not that "above them"
is similar to "between them":
just as "between them" is where she is not touching on top of them,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּבֵּיהֶן – דְּלָא נָגְעָה עֲלַיְיהוּ,
phrases.english: so too "above them" is where she is not touching on top of them,
and that is [the case of] tree branches?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי לָאו עַל גַּבֵּיהֶן, דּוּמְיָא דְּבֵינֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the actual proof from the ברייתא quoted in step 37.
steps.raayaObject: רב's ruling that a bird on branches above the nest obligates.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The parallel between "between them" and "above them" in the ברייתא: both describe a bird not resting on the young, so "above them" means branches, and it is obligated.

steps.title: Above them means touching them, so a bird on branches is exempt
steps.stepSummary: The proof for רב is rejected. 'Above them' is like 'between them' only in that the bird touches the young. A bird resting on tree branches without touching them is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. 'Above them' is like 'between them' in this way: just as 'between them' means she touches them, so too 'above them' means she touches them. But if she sits on tree branches, one is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof for רב from step 38. It reads the comparison between 'above' and 'between' the opposite way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 38 said the common point of 'above' and 'between' is that the bird is not resting on the young. Here the common point is the reverse: in both cases the bird touches the young. So the ברייתא obligates only when she touches them, and a bird on branches is exempt. That is the opposite of רב.

keyTerms.meaning: Similar to, compared with
She touches them (the eggs or chicks)
Tree branches (layers of branches)
Exempt, no obligation

steps.confusionAlert: Both step 38 and this step say 'above them is like between them.' They disagree only about what the two cases share. Step 38 says 'not resting on the young.' This step says 'touching the young.'

phrases.english: No, 'above them' is similar to 'between them':
just as 'between them' is where she touches them,

But tree branches: exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof for רב offered in step 38 by reading the ברייתא's comparison differently.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof for רב from the ברייתא's case of 'above them'.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The comparison of 'above' to 'between' can mean the bird touches the young, not that she is off them. On that reading, branches are exempt.

steps.title: Challenge from the last clause about the hovering bird begins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the new reading. If branches are exempt, why does the last clause of the ברייתא teach the case of a hovering bird whose wings touch the nest? The challenge finishes in the next lines.
steps.simpleTranslation: If that is so, then instead of teaching in the last clause: 'If she was hovering, even if her wings touch the nest, one is exempt'…
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a challenge to the reading in step 39. This line sets up the question, and the rest of the sentence comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 39 says a bird on branches that does not touch the young is exempt. The גמרא questions why the ברייתא's last clause would then use the hovering bird to show an exemption. On this reading, a clearer exemption case seems to be available.

keyTerms.meaning: If so, if that is the case

Hovering, flying over the nest

steps.kashyaTarget: The reading in step 39 that a bird on tree branches is exempt.
